body:
I wanted to pick up and continue a wider conversation here with @lawnjelly and @jrouwe about this waking problem across all physics engines Godot supports. 

## Background
Constraint removal is not a bug per-se. Some engines will ensure that bodies wake automatically on constraint removals and other engines will offer the user some manual controls to achieve a solution.

However, Godot doesn't currently offer either an 'automatic' or 'manual'.

It does offer AABB intersection query functions which you can use to get a list of bodies and then wake them manually. 

However this is both slow and difficult (at least in gdScript and probably C#). I would also like users to have the option of getting 'automatic' behaviour (with full knowledge that it might cause performance hiccups in some cases).

## My proposed plan: 

1. I work on a draft PR for Godot-Jolt to provide whatever is needed to be able to fix the constraint removal issue for Jolt (we already know the high performance approach from Jolt docs, but I want to explore easier options also) 
2. Review of Jolt draft PR by @jrouwe
3. Revisit this Godot Physics 2D draft PR based on learnings
5. Revisit Bullet PR #124422 review based on learnings
7. Copy this Godot Physics 2D 4.x PR to Godot Physics 3D 4.x, and then Godot Physics 2D/3D 3.x
8. Everyone green light's reviews and merges on all these PR's, etc

*Note that PR #124422 could go ahead without aligning with whatever 4.x does, but there could be benefit in waiting.*

*If anyone else wants to fill in any of these steps themselves, I am more than happy with that! ;-) Otherwise I will get plodding along.*

@jrouwe: Are you happy in principal with this? I mean maybe doing a review of my PR for Godot-Jolt? 

If someone more familiar or capable with Jolt is ready to do it then I am all for it, but I am also happy to take a stab at it myself and I feel like there is a lot of code there that I can learn from.

Just to outline some options here:
* manual call (as used in #124422)
* fully automatic (e.g. this PR, #124215)
* optional automatic (either global or per node) and / or manual

The concern raised by @jrouwe with automatic (with no options), as I understood it (could be lost in translation.. :grin: ) is that this could cause performance regressions or performance problems in some situations, and this is very possible (that's what led me to favour #124422 at least initially, over #124215).

> One last performance issue that has been previously discussed is what happens when you dispose of a large amount of bodies all at once.

Would it be possible to try some benchmark tests adding / removing bodies in worst cases so we can see the performance impact (currently)? If there's no significant change, that would seem to help answer our question here.

Other than working out ahead of time whether it will cause problems, if we aren't sure about a PR impact it is common to:
* introduce it in an early beta, ask for testing and wait for feedback, and only introduce mitigations once it has been shown there _is_ a problem (i.e. not an imagined problem)
* introduce it with some kind of on / off switch (which can later be removed if not required)

An additional factor is that once we introduce auto-wakeup functionality, people will start writing games depending on it and it becomes difficult to remove. So it's easy to go from a manual approach -> automatic approach, but we won't be able to revert from an automatic approach -> a manual approach.

And it is notable that many of the major engines seem to have stuck with a manual approach here afaik (they have reports of similar floating objects, and the need to wake manually). That may represent them e.g. "not knowing how best to approach the problem", or it may represent some systemic issues with auto-waking at scale - but the fact there is not a standard solution suggests we should be wary.

Also to repeat a note on your earlier PR:
* this fixes GodotPhysics but we might not be able to get the same behaviour in other backends, especially if this kind of thing is stored in thirdparty code, which we don't want to modify significantly

Feature parity is a good aim if we can achieve it - we ideally don't want to end up in a situation where one backend can do auto-wakeup, but another can't, so users end up having to choose backends based on such a feature, or have barriers to changing physics engine.

### Streaming
I suspect the big area we should be examining as the worst case scenario for auto-waking is _streaming_. We should be aiming to have something where if we have a large chunk of world loaded in (maybe in the background) that physics can load in bodies _without_ waking them, and also remove bodies _without waking_.

This already doesn't work ideally - as I think you noticed elsewhere, bodies seem to be currently woken anyway when first added to the world. But perhaps we should revisit this.

The manual approach neatly gets around most of the problems with streaming, as you are leaving it up to the user when they explicitly want things to start moving.

The other option I investigated briefly is storing an `alive` flag per body, essentially where it is wakeable or not. If we can set this to false during streaming load and streaming save, or deleting levels, we can neatly avoid the auto-wake causing any performance issues. However managing these flags from the Godot side may be a little tricky, but never-the-less, doable.

I have put more research and thought into this (including digging into Jolt and doing more testing). I think below represents a pretty good solution for now because it probably meets user expectations with relatively minimal change. 

This may not address all your comments, and it's not just about this PR. I am just trying to outline a possible new plan for addressing wake issues:

## Current situation
The issue here is about bodies not simulating the way the user would expect because they are not waking up under certain conditions which are usually initiated by the user directly moving kinematic and static bodies:

### Collide
When a body first collides with a sleeping body, does it wake that body? 

### Move
When a body moves away from another sleeping body which is touching it, does that sleeping body wake?

### Free
When a body is deleted or removed from a space, does it wake any bodies that were touching it?

The table below shows how the various engines currently function. 'AUTO' means this case is automatically handled by the engine, and '-' means that bodies will not be woken on this condition.

| Backend                | Move: Static | Move: Kinematic | Free: Both   | Collide: Both |
|------------------------|--------------|-----------------|--------------|---------------|
| Godot Physics 2D/3D    | AUTO         | -               | -            | AUTO          |
| Bullet 3D 3.x          | -            | -               | -            | -             |
| Jolt Physics 3D 4.x    | -            | AUTO            | -            | AUTO          |
| Rapier Physics 2D/3D   | AUTO         | AUTO            | AUTO         | AUTO          |

* Bullet is not waking bodies on 'Collide'. That is unacceptable and should be fixed.
* Godot Physics and Bullet are not waking bodies on 'Move: Kinematic'. That doesn't meet user expectations.

* None of the engines are currently waking neighbors on 'Free: Both', but that is less important IMO. 
* Jolt and Bullet do not currently wake neighbors on 'Move: Static'. That is not so bad, because they can use a kinematic object instead, and it meets existing user expectations. 

See link to Unity docs below where it talks about problems with moving static bodies (this sets user expectations for 3D, which are that they can move kinematic bodies, but static body movement can be undefined):
(https://docs.unity3d.com/6000.6/Documentation/Manual/collider-types-introduction.html)

## I would propose that what we only do the following two fixes for now:

* Godot Physics should wake bodies on constraint removal. This would add effectively zero additional book keeping cost. It adds the expected cost of waking to test if balance has changed, but that is a generally unavoidable simulation cost and the cost will not be paid at all if you are then deleting those bodies. This is what Box2D does, and what I would polish up this PR to do.

* Bullet 3D 3.x: Set kinematic body to DISABLE_DEACTIVATION. This may add some minimal BVH query cost when Kinematic bodies move (but cheaper than a manual AABB wake). I don't think we need to go further than this as it fixes everything for Kinematic bodies (even wake on free for Kinematic bodies in most cases). Only Kinematic bodies need to work fully with user movement, not static. I have submitted a draft PR to show what I mean here #124687. There is a 3.x MRP there also.

After the above changes, the table would look like this:

| Backend                | Move: Static | Move: Kinematic | Free: Both   | Collide: Both |
|------------------------|--------------|-----------------|--------------|---------------|
| Godot Physics 2D/3D    | AUTO         | AUTO            | AUTO         | AUTO          |
| Bullet 3D 3.x          | -            | AUTO            | -            | AUTO          |
| Jolt Physics 3D 4.x    | -            | AUTO            | -            | AUTO          |
| Rapier Physics 2D/3D   | AUTO         | AUTO            | AUTO         | AUTO          |

This would satisfy user expectations for 3D and 2D without doing anything unusual.

## Why not change Godot Physics so that 'Move: Static' and 'Free: Both' don't work

It's possible to explicitly limit Godot physics 2D to match Bullet and Jolt, but that would not fix the issue this PR was initiated for, it would not meet user expectations for 2D Physics, and it would take more code to do so. 

User expectations for 2D are not just set by Unity, but also by Box2D and novice friendly engines like GDevelop that use Box2D V3 and 'just work'.

As a side effect of making Godot Physics 2D 'just work', I would tend to want to fix Godot Physics 3D in the same way to keep it in sync.

## What if users lock in to the Godot 'just works' approach?
They will generally only be doing that for 2D (since 3D users will be using Jolt or Bullet). Users already expect this behaviour for 2D, so we aren't building new expectations, just meeting them.

Also, the 3D behaviour of Jolt and Bullet (with the fix) do 'just work' as long as you are using Kinematic bodies for movement and not expecting wake on delete. If we get issues with this behaviour, then we could come back and look at manual API.

## 3D MRP's for 4.x and 3.x

Below is an MRP for 4.x and 3.x for 3D (extension of the #124422 MRP). I have been using this to test various scenarios.

[wake-neighbours-MRP-4.x.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33706168/wake-neighbours-MRP-4.x.zip)

[wake-neighbours-MRP-3.x.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33706169/wake-neighbours-MRP-3.x.zip)

## Next steps

If this plan is agreeable:

@lawnjelly to review #124687 or consider simplifying #124422 in a similar way for Bullet. Alternatively if #124422 is preferred, let me know and I can review #124422 (but then 3.x would be different to 4.x).

I would need to polish up this PR and then apply it to Godot Physics 3D 4.x and Godot Physics 2D/3D 3.x (if it looks to easily transfer). I also need to pick up any other feedback relevant to this specific PR that I may have missed.
